opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think backtracking is one of the most interesting things we saw when we looked at these reasoning traces. If you go through the samples from models like DeepSeek R1 or Gemini's thinking models, the ones that end up being really useful for training aren't the clean, linear solutions where the model writes step one, step two, step three, and then the answer. The valuable ones are where the model says something like "wait, that doesn't seem right," goes back, and re-checks an earlier step or tries a different approach.

The reason that matters is that it teaches the model a behavior rather than just a solution. If you only train on perfect traces, the model learns to commit to whatever path it starts on. But on hard problems, competition math or tricky science questions, your first attempt is often wrong. A model that has seen lots of examples of noticing an error and correcting it learns that it's allowed, even encouraged, to doubt itself and explore. That's essentially search happening inside the chain of thought.

It also ties into test-time scaling. In our s1 work, one simple trick was that when the model tried to stop thinking, we'd append "Wait" and let it keep going. Very often it would then re-examine its answer and fix a mistake. That only works if the model has learned that backtracking is part of how you reason. So the "Wait" token is a lever that gives you more compute at inference time, and the backtracking behavior in the training data is what makes that extra compute actually turn into better answers.

So with only around a thousand examples, choosing traces that are difficult, diverse, and full of this self-verification is a big part of why such a small dataset can unlock so much reasoning ability. You're not teaching the model new knowledge so much as showing it how to use what it already knows more carefully.

r001.rationale: The response says that on hard problems, a model’s first attempt is often wrong and describes rechecking an earlier step or trying another approach, linking backtracking to especially difficult questions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so backtracking ended up being one of the things that surprised us the most when we were putting together the s1 data. The intuition is pretty simple: if you only train on traces that go straight from the question to the right answer, the model learns to be confident, but it doesn't learn what to do when it's wrong. And in practice, on hard math or science problems, the model is going to be wrong in the middle of its reasoning a lot of the time. The important skill isn't never making a mistake, it's noticing you've made one and recovering from it.

So when we looked at the traces we distilled, the ones that contained phrases like "wait, that's not right" or "let me check this again" were doing something qualitatively different from the clean, linear solutions. The model was essentially verifying its own intermediate steps, catching an arithmetic error or a wrong assumption, and going back to an earlier point to try a different branch. That's the behavior you actually want at test time, because that's what lets you turn more compute into better answers. If the model can't backtrack, giving it a longer budget just means it writes more text down the wrong path.

That connects directly to the budget forcing idea. When we suppress the end-of-thinking token and append "Wait," the only reason that works is that the model has learned that "Wait" is a cue to re-examine what it just did. If the training traces never showed self-correction, that intervention would just produce rambling. So backtracking in the data is kind of what makes test-time scaling meaningful. It gives the model a mechanism for using extra tokens productively rather than just filling space.

And I'd add that it's a small amount of data. We're talking about a thousand examples. So you're not teaching the model new math, it already knows the math from pretraining. You're teaching it a reasoning format, and backtracking is probably the most important part of that format. It's the thing that distinguishes a trace that looks like actual thinking from a trace that looks like a textbook solution.

r001.rationale: The response says that on hard math or science problems the model is often wrong mid-reasoning and must notice and recover, linking backtracking to especially difficult questions.

astra-6.text:
I think backtracking is important because reasoning isn’t always a straight line to the answer. You try an approach, realize that something doesn’t work, and then go back and try something else. That ability to recognize a mistake and recover is part of what we want the model to learn.

If the training traces only show a clean path to the correct answer, they don’t demonstrate what to do when you take a wrong turn. Including backtracking gives the model examples of checking its own reasoning and revising it. The useful part isn’t the mistake itself; it’s recognizing why the approach failed and making progress from there.

r001.rationale: The response describes backtracking as trying an approach, recognizing it failed, and revising reasoning, but does not say it is more likely on especially difficult questions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think backtracking is important because you don’t necessarily know the right approach when you start solving a problem. You might try something, realize it doesn’t work, and then go back and try a different approach. That’s a useful part of reasoning, and we want the model to learn it.

If your training traces only show a clean path to the correct answer, the model doesn’t get examples of how to recognize a mistake or recover from a dead end. Including backtracking gives it a chance to learn that behavior—to question an intermediate result, revise its approach, and keep making progress instead of just continuing down the wrong path.

r001.rationale: The response describes backtracking after an approach fails, but does not say it is more likely when tackling especially difficult questions.
